Error t value Pr(>|t|) ## (Intercept) 251.405 6.610 38.033 < 2e-16 *** ## days 10.467 1.238 8.454 9.89e-15 *** ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ## ## Residual standard error: 47.71 on 178 degrees of freedom ## Multiple R-squared: 0.2865, Adjusted R-squared: 0.2825 ## F-statistic: 71.46 on 1 and 178 DF, p-value: 9.894e-15 This model is not accounting for the fact that we have repeated measurements for each subject. It is treating each observation as independent, which is not the case. This can lead to underestimated standard errors and inflated type I error rates. We need a way to account for the fact that we have repeated measurements for each subject, and that the intercepts and slopes may vary by subject. This is where mixed models come in, which we will cover in the next lecture. 9.7 February 19 9.7.1 Random Slopes When we have one predictor with random intercepts and slopes, the model can be written like this: \[ y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ij} + b_{0i} + b_{1i} x_{ij} + \epsilon_{ij} \] where \(b_{0i}\) is the random intercept for group \(i\), and \(b_{1i}\) is the random slope for predictor \(x\) in group \(i\). We assume that the random effects \((b_{0i}, b_{1i})\) are jointly normally distributed with mean 0 and covariance matrix \(\Sigma\), and that the errors \(\epsilon_{ij}\) are normally distributed with mean 0 and variance \(\sigma^2\). The random effects and errors are assumed to be independent of each other. Note that we could also combine the fixed effects with the random effects to say that the intercept has mean \(\beta_0\) and the slope has mean \(\beta_1\), together with the covariance informarion. We can fit the data by using lmer as follows: mod <- lme4::lmer(reaction ~ days + (1 + days|subject), data = ss) summary(mod) ## Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod'] ## Formula: reaction ~ days + (1 + days | subject) ## Data: ss ## ## REML criterion at convergence: 1743.6 ## ## Scaled residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -3.9536 -0.4634 0.0231 0.4634 5.1793 ## ## Random effects: ## Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. Corr ## subject (Intercept) 612.10 24.741 ## days 35.07 5.922 0.07 ## Residual 654.94 25.592 ## Number of obs: 180, groups: subject, 18 ## ## Fixed effects: ## Estimate Std. Error t value ## (Intercept) 251.405 6.825 36.838 ## days 10.467 1.546 6.771 ## ## Correlation of Fixed Effects: ## (Intr) ## days -0.138 We obtain the following estimates for the parameters of the model: \(\hat \beta_0 = 251.405\) (mean intercept across subjects) \(\hat \beta_1 = 10.467\) (mean slope across subjects) \(\hat \tau_0^2 = 612.1\) (variance of random intercepts) \(\hat \tau_1^2 = 35\) (variance of random slopes) \(\hat \sigma^2 = 654.94\) (variance of residuals) \(\hat \rho = 0.07\) (correlation between random intercepts and slopes) Note that this model has one additional parameter which we didn’t specify in our mathematical model above, which is the correlation between random intercepts and slopes. A positive value for this correlation indicates that subjects with higher baseline reaction times (higher random intercepts) tend to have steeper increases in reaction time with more days of sleep deprivation (higher random slopes), while a negative value would indicate the opposite. In this case, the correlation is close to zero, suggesting that there is little relationship between the random intercepts and slopes in this data set. If we want to fit a model that does not include the correlation, we can use the following: mod <- lme4::lmer(reaction ~ days + (1 + days||subject), data = ss) #the || syntax forces the correlation to be zero summary(mod) ## Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod'] ## Formula: reaction ~ days + ((1 | subject) + (0 + days | subject)) ## Data: ss ## ## REML criterion at convergence: 1743.7 ## ## Scaled residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -3.9626 -0.4625 0.0204 0.4653 5.1860 ## ## Random effects: ## Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. ## subject (Intercept) 627.57 25.051 ## subject.1 days 35.86 5.988 ## Residual 653.58 25.565 ## Number of obs: 180, groups: subject, 18 ## ## Fixed effects: ## Estimate Std. Error t value ## (Intercept) 251.405 6.885 36.513 ## days 10.467 1.560 6.712 ## ## Correlation of Fixed Effects: ## (Intr) ## days -0.184 There is very little change in the estimated parameter values. One interesting question that can be asked with a model with random slopes is: what proportion of subjects have a positive slope? In other words, what proportion of subjects have reaction times that increase with more days of sleep deprivation? We can answer this question by looking at the distribution of the random slopes. random_slopes <- ranef(mod)$subject$days #this gives us the random slope for each subject mean_slope <- fixef(mod)["days"] #this gives us the fixed effect slope #the total slope for each subject is the fixed effect slope plus the random slope for that subject total_slopes <- mean_slope + random_slopes total_slopes ## [1] 19.7907830 1.8681102 5.0794915 5.4986357 7.2733482 10.1587920 ## [7] 10.1800781 11.5832770 -0.4386895 19.0949087 11.7479752 17.2236923 ## [13] 7.3921504 13.9794982 11.3403373 15.4510769 9.4619922 11.7256896 What is our estimate of the total percentage of the total population that has a negative slope? We can use the normal distribution to answer this question, because the random slopes are assumed to be normally distributed. pnorm(0, mean = mean_slope, sd = sqrt(35)) #35 is the variance of the random slopes, so we take the square root to get the standard deviation ## [1] 0.03842239 We see that about 4 percent of the population is estimated to have a negative slope, which means that their reaction times decrease with more days of sleep deprivation. This is an interesting finding, and it highlights the importance of looking at the random effects in a mixed model, rather than just the fixed effects. The fixed effect tells us about the average effect across all subjects, but the random effects tell us about the variability in the effect across subjects. In this case, while the average effect of days of sleep deprivation on reaction time is positive, there is a small proportion of subjects for whom the effect is negative. What is a confidence interval for the main slope effect? We can use the standard error of the fixed effect slope to construct a confidence interval. The standard error is given in the summary output of the model, or we can use emmeans or lmerTest to get it. Let’s use lmerTest to get the confidence interval. library(lmerTest) mod2 <- lmerTest::lmer(reaction ~ days + (1 + days||subject), data = ss) summary(mod2) ## Linear mixed model fit by REML. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method [ ## lmerModLmerTest] ## Formula: reaction ~ days + (1 + days || subject) ## Data: ss ## ## REML criterion at convergence: 1743.7 ## ## Scaled residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -3.9626 -0.4625 0.0204 0.4653 5.1860 ## ## Random effects: ## Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. ## subject (Intercept) 627.57 25.051 ## subject.1 days 35.86 5.988 ## Residual 653.58 25.565 ## Number of obs: 180, groups: subject, 18 ## ## Fixed effects: ## Estimate Std. For example, we can compare the model with random slopes to the model without random slopes, or we can compare the model with random slopes and random intercepts to the model with only random intercepts. We can also compare the model with correlated random effects to the model with uncorrelated random effects. Let’s see how to do this in R. mod_random_slopes <- lmer(reaction ~ days + (1 + days|subject), data = ss) mod_random_intercepts <- lmer(reaction ~ days + (1|subject), data = ss) anova(mod_random_intercepts, mod_random_slopes) ## refitting model(s) with ML (instead of REML) ## Data: ss ## Models: ## mod_random_intercepts: reaction ~ days + (1 | subject) ## mod_random_slopes: reaction ~ days + (1 + days | subject) ## npar AIC BIC logLik -2*log(L) Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq) ## mod_random_intercepts 4 1802.1 1814.8 -897.04 1794.1 ## mod_random_slopes 6 1763.9 1783.1 -875.97 1751.9 42.139 2 7.072e-10 ## ## mod_random_intercepts ## mod_random_slopes *** ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 In general, the null hypothesis being tested is that all of the extra parameters in the larger model are zero versus at least one of the parameters is not zero. So, a \(p\)-value less than 0.05 is evidence that the larger model is a significantly better fit to the data than the smaller model, which suggests that at least one of the extra parameters in the larger model is not zero. In this case, we are testing whether the variance of the random slopes is zero, which is equivalent to testing whether the random slopes are necessary to explain the variability in the data. If we reject the null hypothesis, we can conclude that there is significant variability in the slopes across subjects, and that the model with random slopes fits significantly better than the model with only random intercepts. If we fail to reject the null hypothesis, we can conclude that there is not enough evidence to suggest that there is significant variability in the slopes across subjects, and that the model with only random intercepts may be sufficient to explain the variability in the data. We can also look at the AIC or BIC values for the two models, which are measures of model fit that penalize for the number of parameters in the model. The model with the lower AIC or BIC value is generally considered to be the better fitting model. In this case, we would expect the model with random slopes to have a lower AIC and BIC value than the model with only random intercepts, which would further support the conclusion that the model with random slopes fits significantly better than the model with only random intercepts. We conclude that the model with random slopes fits significantly better than the model with only random intercepts, which suggests that there is significant variability in the slopes across subjects. We can also compare the model with correlated random effects to the model with uncorrelated random effects. Now let’s compare the model with correlated random effects to the model with uncorrelated random effects. mod_correlated <- lmer(reaction ~ days + (1 + days|subject), data = ss, REML = F) mod_uncorrelated <- lmer(reaction ~ days + (1 + days||subject), data = ss, REML = F) anova(mod_uncorrelated, mod_correlated) ## Data: ss ## Models: ## mod_uncorrelated: reaction ~ days + (1 + days || subject) ## mod_correlated: reaction ~ days + (1 + days | subject) ## npar AIC BIC logLik -2*log(L) Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq) ## mod_uncorrelated 5 1762.0 1778.0 -876.00 1752.0 ## mod_correlated 6 1763.9 1783.1 -875.97 1751.9 0.0639 1 0.8004 The model with uncorrelated random effects fits significantly better than the model with correlated random effects, which suggests that there is not a significant correlation between the random intercepts and random slopes in this data set. This is consistent with the estimate of the correlation that we obtained from the model with correlated random effects, which was close to zero. When we have different fixed effects, we should not use REML = T to compare the models, because the fixed effects are different. Note that anova will fix this for us if we forget. mod <- lmer(reaction ~ days + (1|subject), data = ss, REML = F) mod2 <- lmer(reaction ~ 1 + (1|subject), data = ss, REML = F) anova(mod2, mod) ## Data: ss ## Models: ## mod2: reaction ~ 1 + (1 | subject) ## mod: reaction ~ days + (1 | subject) ## npar AIC BIC logLik -2*log(L) Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq) ## mod2 3 1916.5 1926.1 -955.27 1910.5 ## mod 4 1802.1 1814.8 -897.04 1794.1 116.46 1 < 2.2e-16 *** ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 The model with the fixed effect of days fits significantly better than the model with only a random intercept. We can re-run this with REML = T and see we get the same answer, with a message. mod <- lmer(reaction ~ days + (1|subject), data = ss, REML = T) mod2 <- lmer(reaction ~ 1 + (1|subject), data = ss, REML = T) anova(mod2, mod) ## refitting model(s) with ML (instead of REML) ## Data: ss ## Models: ## mod2: reaction ~ 1 + (1 | subject) ## mod: reaction ~ days + (1 | subject) ## npar AIC BIC logLik -2*log(L) Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq) ## mod2 3 1916.5 1926.1 -955.27 1910.5 ## mod 4 1802.1 1814.8 -897.04 1794.1 116.46 1 < 2.2e-16 *** ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 9.7.3 Some Theory How does lmer estimate the parameters in our models? lmer uses maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) to estimate the parameters of the model. The likelihood function is based on the assumption that the random effects and the residuals are normally distributed. The MLE approach finds the parameter values that maximize the likelihood of observing the data given the model. In practice, lmer uses an optimization algorithm to find the parameter values that maximize the likelihood function, which can be computationally intensive for complex models with many parameters. The estimation process involves iteratively updating the parameter estimates until convergence is achieved, meaning that further updates do not significantly change the parameter estimates. Let’s look at an example. ss <- lme4::sleepstudy |> janitor::clean_names() |> as_tibble() We estimate the parameters involved with a random intercepts model. To set notation, the mathematical formulation of this model is \[ \text{reaction}_{ij} = \gamma_{00} + \beta_1 \text{days}_{ij} + u_{0i} + \epsilon_{ij} \] We can start by getting reasonable guesses for the values. mod <- lm(reaction ~ days + subject, data = ss) summary(mod) ## ## Call: ## lm(formula = reaction ~ days + subject, data = ss) ## ## Residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -100.540 -16.389 -0.341 15.215 131.159 ## ## Coefficients: ## Estimate Std. The final estimated value will likely be smaller than this. Let’s see what lmer gives. mod_lmer <- lme4::lmer(reaction ~ days + (1|subject), data = ss) summary(mod_lmer) ## Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod'] ## Formula: reaction ~ days + (1 | subject) ## Data: ss ## ## REML criterion at convergence: 1786.5 ## ## Scaled residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -3.2257 -0.5529 0.0109 0.5188 4.2506 ## ## Random effects: ## Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. ## subject (Intercept) 1378.2 37.12 ## Residual 960.5 30.99 ## Number of obs: 180, groups: subject, 18 ## ## Fixed effects: ## Estimate Std. Error t value ## (Intercept) 251.4051 9.7467 25.79 ## days 10.4673 0.8042 13.02 ## ## Correlation of Fixed Effects: ## (Intr) ## days -0.371 Our values are pretty close. We can use these values as starting points for the optimization algorithm that lmer uses to find the MLE estimates. Using our mathematical model of reaction, we can see that each response is a function of the fixed effects, the random effects, and the residuals. The distribution of a single response is \[ y_{ij} \sim N(\gamma_{00} + \beta_1 x_{ij}, \tau^2 + \sigma^2) \] where here we use the assumption that \(u_{0i} \sim N(0, \tau^2)\) and \(\epsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\) are independent. The likelihood function is the product of the probability density functions for each response, which is a function of the parameters \(\gamma_{00}\), \(\beta_1\), \(\tau^2\), and \(\sigma^2\). The MLE estimates are the values of these parameters that maximize the likelihood function. When we do this, we will maximize the log of the likelihood function, in order to keep values reasonably sized. #This isn't correct like <- function(par) { gamma <- par[1] beta <- par[2] tau2 <- par[3] sigma2 <- par[4] mu <- gamma + beta * ss$days var <- tau2 + sigma2 -sum(dnorm(ss$reaction, mean = mu, sd = sqrt(var), log = TRUE)) } like(c(295, 10.5, 1474, 961)) ## [1] 1021.136 oo <- optim(par = c(295, 10.5, 1474, 961), fn = like, method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = c(-Inf, -Inf, 0, 0)) like(oo$par) ## [1] 950.1465 tidy_modlmer <- broom.mixed::tidy(mod_lmer) like(c(tidy_modlmer$estimate[1], tidy_modlmer$estimate[2], tidy_modlmer$estimate[3]^2, tidy_modlmer$estimate[4]^2)) ## [1] 950.2107 We can see that we don’t quite get the fully correct answer. This is because we haven’t correctly described the likelihood function for a mixed effect model. The likelihood function for a mixed effect model is more complicated than the one we wrote down above, because it allows correlation within subjects. The likelihood function for a mixed effect model is based on the joint distribution of the responses for each subject, which is a multivariate normal distribution with mean vector and covariance matrix that depend on the fixed effects and the random effects. While the marginal distribution of each response is normal, the joint distribution of the responses for each subject is multivariate normal with correlation between responses from the same subject. Let’s see how it works. par <- oo$par library(mvtnorm) nll <- function(par) { gamma <- par[1] beta <- par[2] tau2 <- par[3] sigma2 <- par[4] if (tau2 < 0 || sigma2 <= 0) return(Inf) response <- ss$reaction pred_fixed_effect <- gamma + beta * ss$days #this is the same as mu, which is a good check g <- factor(ss$subject) #this is the grouping variable for the random intercepts) Z <- model.matrix(~ 0 + g) # columns correspond to groups (levels of g) N <- length(response) V <- tau2 * (Z %*% t(Z)) + sigma2 * diag(N) # Marginal covariance: V = tau2 * Z Z' + sigma2 * I_N -dmvnorm(response, mean = pred_fixed_effect, sigma = V, log = TRUE) } nll(par) ## [1] 897.4195 optim(par = par, fn = nll, method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = c(-Inf, -Inf, 0, 0)) ## $par ## [1] 251.40703 10.46715 1379.07124 954.27973 ## ## $value ## [1] 897.0538 ## ## $counts ## function gradient ## 15 15 ## ## $convergence ## [1] 0 ## ## $message ## [1] "CONVERGENCE: REL_REDUCTION_OF_F <= FACTR*EPSMCH" summary(mod_lmer) ## Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod'] ## Formula: reaction ~ days + (1 | subject) ## Data: ss ## ## REML criterion at convergence: 1786.5 ## ## Scaled residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -3.2257 -0.5529 0.0109 0.5188 4.2506 ## ## Random effects: ## Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. ## subject (Intercept) 1378.2 37.12 ## Residual 960.5 30.99 ## Number of obs: 180, groups: subject, 18 ## ## Fixed effects: ## Estimate Std. Error t value ## (Intercept) 251.4051 9.7467 25.79 ## days 10.4673 0.8042 13.02 ## ## Correlation of Fixed Effects: ## (Intr) ## days -0.371 Aside: Multivariate Normal Distribution When we have random slopes, we need to consider the joint distribution of the random intercepts and slopes. This is typically assumed to be a multivariate normal distribution. The multivariate normal distribution is a generalization of the univariate normal distribution to multiple dimensions. It is defined by a mean vector and a covariance matrix. The mean vector gives the expected value of each variable, while the covariance matrix gives the variance of each variable and the covariance between each pair of variables. Let’s look at an example: Sigma <- matrix(c(3, 2, 2, 5), nrow = 2) eigen(Sigma) #this is a positive definite matrix, so it is a valid covariance matrix ## eigen() decomposition ## $values ## [1] 6.236068 1.763932 ## ## $vectors ## [,1] [,2] ## [1,] 0.5257311 -0.8506508 ## [2,] 0.8506508 0.5257311 dd <- data.frame(MASS::mvrnorm(n = 1000, mu = c(1, 4), Sigma = Sigma)) ggplot(dd, aes(x = X1, y = X2)) + geom_point() + coord_equal() To force independence of the coordinates, we set the covariances equal to zero. Note that for general rvs, uncorrelated does not imply independent, but for multivariate normal rvs, uncorrelated does imply independent. This is why we get a zero estimate for the variance of the random intercepts, which is likely not the true value, but rather an artifact of the limited data we have for this particular mark. Chapter 10 Solutions 10.1 Chapter 2 Solutions Exercise 2.1 We have that \(\overline{X}\) is normal with mean \(\overline{\mu}\) and variance \(\frac 1{25}\sum \sigma_i^2\), i.e. \(\overline{X} \sim N(3, \sigma^2 = 2.2)\). To confirm this via simulations: sim_data <- replicate(10000, { x <- rnorm(5, 1:5, sqrt((1:5)^2)) mean(x) }) mean(sim_data) #cf 3 ## [1] 3.020358 var(sim_data) #cf 2.2 ## [1] 2.200486 plot(density(sim_data)) curve(dnorm(x, 3, sqrt(2.2)), add = T, col = 2) Exercise 2.2 bp.obese <- ISwR::bp.obese sse <- function(beta) { sum((bp.obese$bp - (beta[1] + beta[2] * bp.obese$obese))^2) } optim(par = c(0,0), fn = sse) ## $par ## [1] 96.80371 23.01824 ## ## $value ## [1] 29845.55 ## ## $counts ## function gradient ## 109 NA ## ## $convergence ## [1] 0 ## ## $message ## NULL Our line of best fit is \(y = 96.8 + 23 x\). Confirm with lm: lm(bp ~ obese, data = bp.obese) ## ## Call: ## lm(formula = bp ~ obese, data = bp.obese) ## ## Coefficients: ## (Intercept) obese ## 96.82 23.00 For part (b), either answer is OK. The data seems pretty good to me, but I can see where some people didn’t think so. As long as you say why. Exercise 2.3 Note that \(\sum_{i = 1}^n \beta_0 = n\beta_0\). The solution is \(\hat \beta_0 = \overline{y} - \overline{x}\). \(\hat \beta_0\) is normal with mean \(\beta_0\) and variance \(\sigma^2/n\). Let’s simulate. xs <- runif(20, 0, 10) sim_data <- replicate(10000, { ys <- 2 + xs + rnorm(20, 0, 1) mean(ys) - mean(xs) }) plot(density(sim_data)) curve(dnorm(x, 2, 1/sqrt(20)), add = T, col = 2) Exercise 2.4 We have that \[ \frac{\hat \beta_1 - \beta_1}{\sqrt{nS^2/(n\sum x_i^2 - (\sum x_i)^2)}} \sim t_{n -2} \] So we compute. dd <- HistData::Galton mod <- lm(child ~ parent, data = dd) summary(mod) ## ## Call: ## lm(formula = child ~ parent, data = dd) ## ## Residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -7.8050 -1.3661 0.0487 1.6339 5.9264 ## ## Coefficients: ## Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) ## (Intercept) 23.94153 2.81088 8.517 <2e-16 *** ## parent 0.64629 0.04114 15.711 <2e-16 *** ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ## ## Residual standard error: 2.239 on 926 degrees of freedom ## Multiple R-squared: 0.2105, Adjusted R-squared: 0.2096 ## F-statistic: 246.8 on 1 and 926 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 The estimate for \(S\) is given as 2.239, which we use. We compute the test statistic: (0.64629 - 1)/sqrt(2.239^2/(sum(dd$parent^2) - 1/928 * sum(dd$parent)^2)) ## [1] -8.596837 The test statistic is -8.596837. We need to compute the likelihood of obtaining something that unlikely given that \(H_0\) is true. pt(-8.596837, 926) * 2 ## [1] 3.454205e-17 With this \(p\)-value, we reject the null hypothesis. We conlcude that the slope is not 1. With more work, we can see that this means (roughly) that parents who are short or tall will tend to have children that are again short or tall, but less so than the parents. Does that mean that eventually there will be little variation among heights of humans. Why or why not? Exercise 2.5 An unbiased estimator for \(S^2\) is \[ \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{ i = 1}^n \bigl(y_i - \hat\beta_0 - x_i\bigr)^2 \] Standard normal. \(t\) with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom. dd <- read.csv("https://stat.slu.edu/~speegle/Spring2020/4870/data/problem_2_5.csv") beta_0 <- mean(dd$ys) - mean(dd$xs) s <- sqrt(1/(nrow(dd) - 1) * sum((dd$ys - beta_0 - dd$xs)^2)) test_stat <- (beta_0 - 2)/(s/sqrt(nrow(dd))) test_stat ## [1] 2.386556 pt(test_stat, nrow(dd) - 1, lower.tail = FALSE) * 2 ## [1] 0.03167356 Note that this is the same as a paired \(t\)-test, where we have as our null hypothesis that \(y_i - x_i\) is normal with mean 2 and unknown standard deviation. t.test(dd$ys, dd$xs, mu = 2, paired = T) ## ## Paired t-test ## ## data: dd$ys and dd$xs ## t = 2.3866, df = 14, p-value = 0.03167 ## alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 2 ## 95 percent confidence interval: ## 2.121984 4.286277 ## sample estimates: ## mean difference ## 3.204131 Exercise 2.6 dd <- carData::Davis plot(dd$repwt, dd$weight) mod_lm <- lm(weight ~ repwt, data = dd) mod_huber <- MASS::rlm(weight ~ repwt, data = dd, psi = MASS::psi.huber) mod_tukey <- MASS::rlm(weight ~ repwt, data = dd, psi = MASS::psi.bisquare) plot(dd$repwt, dd$weight) abline(mod_lm, col = 2) #red abline(mod_huber, col = 3) #green abline(mod_tukey, col = 4) #blue 10.2 Chapter 3 Solutions Let’s load the data. secher <- ISwR::secher plot(secher[,-4]) mod <- lm(bwt ~ bpd + ad, data = secher) summary(mod) ## ## Call: ## lm(formula = bwt ~ bpd + ad, data = secher) ## ## Residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -607.44 -202.27 -34.89 150.80 1258.45 ## ## Coefficients: ## Estimate Std. Both of these are what we would like to see. 10.3 Chapter 5 Let’s load the data. set.seed(2252020) library(AppliedPredictiveModeling) data("ChemicalManufacturingProcess") The problem asks us to do an initial test/train split and work with the train data from there on out. I’ll pull out the test data and leave the train data with the same variable name. test_indices <- sample(1:176, 46) test_dat <- ChemicalManufacturingProcess[test_indices,] ChemicalManufacturingProcess <- ChemicalManufacturingProcess[-test_indices,] The data isn’t in the format that the book said it would be in. Let’s create a matrix of predictors and a vector response, in addition to the data frame with both. predictors <- ChemicalManufacturingProcess[,-1] response <- ChemicalManufacturingProcess[,1] Now let’s see about missing data. sum(is.na(predictors)) ## [1] 88 We do have missing data, so we will need to preprocess. The first part of the problem asks us to do Principle Component Regression. Let’s do it using the caret package. library(caret) ## Loading required package: ggplot2 ## Loading required package: lattice train(x = predictors, y = response, method = "pcr", preProcess = c("center", "scale", "medianImpute", "nzv")) ## Principal Component Analysis ## ## 130 samples ## 57 predictor ## ## Pre-processing: centered (56), scaled (56), median imputation (56), remove (1) ## Resampling: Bootstrapped (25 reps) ## Summary of sample sizes: 130, 130, 130, 130, 130, 130, ... ## Resampling results across tuning parameters: ## ## ncomp RMSE Rsquared MAE ## 1 1.923932 0.2143977 1.453886 ## 2 1.931708 0.2811579 1.376702 ## 3 2.100334 0.2650185 1.393008 ## ## RMSE was used to select the optimal model using the smallest value. ## The final value used for the model was ncomp = 1. I think we need to expand our tune grid a bit. tuneGrid <- data.frame(ncomp = 1:20) pca_mod <- train(x = predictors, y = response, method = "pcr", tuneGrid = tuneGrid, preProcess = c("center", "scale", "medianImpute", "nzv")) apply(pca_mod$results[,c(2, 5)], 1, sum) ## 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 ## 2.538925 2.217215 2.620412 2.848612 3.369809 3.308128 3.522237 3.580313 ## 9 10 11 12 13 14 15 16 ## 3.180316 3.338443 3.340587 3.059151 3.000264 2.828649 2.497024 2.321957 ## 17 18 19 20 ## 2.285783 2.486719 2.498090 2.882467 The smallest value 1 se away from the estimated MSE is 2.2172154. So, by our one se rule of them, we will choose ncomp <- which(pca_mod$results[,2] < min(apply(pca_mod$results[,c(2, 5)], 1, sum))) ncomp <- min(ncomp) ncomp ## [1] 1 This says that we need one component, and our estimate for the MSE is roughly \(2.1 \pm .92\). pca_mod$results[1,2] ## [1] 2.07493 pca_mod$results[1,5] ## [1] 0.4639948 Let’s check it out on our test set that we haven’t touched yet. We first have to apply the same pre-processing steps to the test data as we did to the train data. preprocess_mod <- preProcess(predictors, method = c("scale", "center", "medianImpute", "nzv")) test_predictors <- test_dat[,-1] test_response <- test_dat[,1] test_processed <- predict(preprocess_mod, newdata = test_predictors) Now we can predict the outcomes on the test set. predict(pca_mod$finalModel, newdata = test_processed, ncomp = 1)[,,1] ## 117 133 96 102 169 20 55 146 ## 39.93165 39.74174 40.10136 39.30054 41.14235 41.81163 40.79884 39.44937 ## 37 110 94 73 88 115 123 157 ## 40.45314 39.15261 40.59883 40.08035 39.65718 39.45967 39.87382 39.39827 ## 35 57 176 49 164 158 70 138 ## 40.92926 40.33136 41.02257 41.98764 39.31417 39.31910 40.22380 38.95523 ## 80 132 95 121 153 11 98 105 ## 40.32705 40.15179 40.18415 38.89349 39.57619 41.29336 40.03982 39.59950 ## 114 23 26 77 118 76 66 51 ## 39.88256 40.17518 40.30996 40.18995 39.22107 40.53561 40.15405 40.77907 ## 54 68 60 100 17 109 ## 40.39532 40.30252 40.63361 39.44431 41.76909 39.70861 errors <- predict(pca_mod$finalModel, newdata = test_processed, ncomp = 1)[,,1] - test_response mean(errors^2) ## [1] 2.621208 This value is within 2 se of the predicted value based on CV.
